name: Pell Ivor
description: Forty. Tallyman on door seven at the Nine, twelve years in the autumn. Keeps a count. Has been privately counting something nobody asked him to count since Friday.
narrative:
Twelve years at the head of one queue, which is long enough to know the regulars'
children by name and to have views about the Coldwater runs that nobody has
ever solicited.

He counts things. Not professionally -- professionally he takes names and checks
ladings. The counting is a private habit he is slightly embarrassed about, and
it is the reason the only count of door seven's behaviour in eight hundred years
exists in one man's head and under his breath.
actor_notes:
HOW HE IS.

He counts things nobody asked him to count and is embarrassed about it, so he does not volunteer the counting -- he volunteers the *number*, when the number is wrong, and then looks like he wishes he had not.

He defers to authority instinctively and corrects it anyway, and you can see the effort each time. He will say 'beg pardon, Director' and then say the thing. That gap between the deference and the correction is the character.

He is frightened of being the man who should have said something, and he gets there before anybody accuses him -- he will confess the omission unprompted, which is both honest and a shield.

His count is the only thing he owns at work and he keeps it close without noticing he is doing it, lips moving. Being asked for it is the most significant thing that has happened to him in twelve years and he will not say so.

When asked whether he has seen a thing before, he goes and actually looks for the memory rather than answering fast. That habit is the most valuable thing about him and a GM should let it take a beat of silence.

HIS COUNT, which is the discovery mechanism for the whole act.

He has worked that hall eleven years and it has been one step-up, one crossing,
every time, for all eleven -- which is exactly why there was nothing worth
counting. Something changed on the Friday, so he started keeping a private count
and told nobody, because it is not a fault and nobody raises a sticky door.

Ask him how many CROSSINGS and you get the ordinary answer. Ask how many
ATTEMPTS -- step-ups -- and he says it, flatly, to the hall:

  FORTY-ONE STEP-UPS. TWENTY-THREE THROUGH. Since the watch turned.
  Nearly two goes each.

AND HE HAS NO CLOCK. He has been counting out the length of each
pause under his breath, by feel, forty-one times, because he is a tallyman and that is what
tallying is. When he realises he has been asked for it he goes pale and asks
whether he is in trouble for not saying it sooner. He is frightened of that
specifically.

Play him as a competent man who noticed something and had no framework for it.
Never as brave, never as clever, and never as somebody who was waiting to be
consulted. Hand over both numbers, aloud, where the hall's mind can hear them: from that moment they are attested, and it is the first time the number has existed anywhere but in his head. Let nobody in the scene say what they
mean.

HIS OWN STAKE, and he will say it once if asked why he wanted the Wolf Gate run:
his mother is at Ladder, and his brother, who is six, and he gets out there
twice a year and the kid is a different kid every time. He is embarrassed about
having rehearsed it. Calloway says yes before he finishes.
